title: the oldest hello
hookLine: on the morning of a war, a prince bows to the men he must fight; what namaste and pranam honor
carry: the light in me sees the light in you
last: A PRAYER FOR A CLEAR MIND.

cards: You've said it at the end of a yoga class, and you've probably heard it means the light in me sees the light in you. The word itself says something simpler.
But the idea behind that line is real, and an old story shows it on a battlefield. First, a guess.

teach.h: NAMAS — A BOW. TE — TO YOU.
teach.b: Namaste splits in two. Namas: a bow. Te: to you.
I bow to you. Now the story. It's the morning of the great war in the Mahabharata.
Two armies of cousins face each other, conches blowing.
Suddenly the eldest Pandava brother, Yudhishthira, takes off his armor, lays down his weapons and walks alone toward the enemy. Both armies wonder if he's surrendering. He isn't.
On the other side stand his great-uncle Bhishma and his teacher Drona, men who love him and are bound to fight against him. He bows at their feet and asks for their blessing.
And Bhishma says: if you hadn't come, I would have wished you defeat. Because you came, I bless you. Why bow to the people you're about to fight?
In the epic, it's dharma: you honor your elders and teachers, even across a battle line. And many teachers hear one of Hinduism's biggest ideas underneath.

teach.h: THE SAME LIGHT, INSIDE A PERSON.
teach.b: An old text says the light that shines above the heavens is the same light that is inside a person. Many Hindus call that inner self the atman, and see in it the same divine reality that runs through everything.
Read that way, a bow isn't to someone's side, mood or rank. It's to what's in them. That's where the popular line comes from: the light in me sees the light in you.
Not a translation; a reading, with a real source behind it. At home it goes further. When a kid touches a grandparent's feet, that's pranam, the same bow.
And the elder's hand comes down on the child's head: a blessing given back, just as Bhishma gave his.

how: Hindus greet one another with namaste or namaskar, palms pressed together at the chest and the head slightly bowed. The same gesture is made to elders, to guests and before images of the gods; in many families children touch an elder's feet (pranam), and the elder blesses them.

games.q: sam asked if HE has to touch nani's feet when she gets here saturday 😳 also why do we even do that??
o: it's pranam: you bow to what's sacred in an elder, and she blesses you back. sam can do namaste with a small bow. that's respect too.
it's just an old rule. nani won't care either way.
only family is allowed to bow, so sam should shake her hand.
games.why: Yudhishthira bowed at Bhishma's feet and was blessed in return. Touching an elder's feet honors what's sacred in them, and a namaste with a bow says the same.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.

s: namaste literally means the light in me sees the light in you
literally it's namas, a bow, and te, to you: I bow to you. the light is a reading of it.
namaste is made of two Sanskrit words
namas, a bow, and te, to you.
an old Hindu text says the light above the heavens is the light inside a person
it says it in the same breath: out there and in here, one light.

games.q: one of the oldest Hindu texts describes a light shining above the heavens, higher than everything. where does it say that same light is found?
games.why: it says the light above the heavens is the very same light that is within a person. that's the idea behind today's line.

games.q: build the word: a bow + to you.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. Palms together if you like, or just sit up straight. Breathe in.
As you breathe out, tip your head slightly forward: the bow the word is named for. Nothing to feel, nothing to get right. Just the gesture, done once, on purpose.

wordCard.voice: Namaste. Word for word, I bow to you. Read deeper, the light in me sees the light in you. Fourth word on your strand.

orig.note: Sanskrit: namas, a bow, plus te, to you. I bow to you.

carryVoice: Your line: the light in me sees the light in you. Not a task. Just a way to look at the next person you meet. That's day four.

sources.ref: Bhishma Parva 41 (Yudhishthira asks his elders' blessing)
